name: Content Prototyping
contentMarkdown:
# Content Prototyping

Content prototyping tests a proposed content or object model by creating representative records and using them in realistic tasks. It helps teams discover missing fields, unclear relationships, and awkward authoring rules before investing in detailed interface design.

In OOUX, a content prototype can make an object map concrete. A spreadsheet, linked database, or simple content-management setup can be sufficient when it supports the questions being tested.

## What are you testing?

The model describes types, fields, and connections. A content prototype populates that structure with instances and examines whether people can create, maintain, and use them.

It can reveal that an apparently simple “status” field contains several different meanings, or that a shared value has been copied into records that need separate ownership.

## Example: populating a travel operations model

An illustrative prototype contains these records:

| Record | Representative content | Question to test |
|---|---|---|
| Trip T-104 | Two travelers and two bookings | Can staff identify the services and people associated with the trip? |
| Booking B-52 | Confirmed, with a supplier confirmation number | Can staff find the information needed to investigate it? |
| Booking B-53 | Awaiting confirmation, with no supplier confirmation number yet | Do required-field rules permit this valid state? |
| Traveler record | A name longer than the usual display examples | Can the same person be recognized across records and views? |

Create more than one record per type where variation matters. Add an empty trip, several related bookings, and a relevant exception.

Use fictional or appropriately redacted content. Preserve the structural characteristics needed for the test.

## A lightweight process

1. Define the questions the prototype must answer.
2. Populate fields and references with representative examples.
3. Ask domain users to create, find, update, and explain records.
4. Record missing information, ambiguous labels, and failed rules.
5. Revise the model and repeat the affected task.

Keep unresolved rules visible. A successful demonstration using only ideal records can hide the cases the model most needs to support.

## Content prototype or interface prototype?

A content prototype primarily tests structure, content, and authoring. An interactive prototype can test placement, navigation, and behavior. They can be combined as the design develops.

A structurally valid record does not establish that a finished screen is usable. Use [OOUX prototyping and testing](/glossary/ooux-prototyping-and-testing.html) to examine how people recognize objects and act on them in the interface.

## Related terms

- [Content Modeling](/glossary/content-modeling.html)
- [Object Mapping](/glossary/object-mapping.html)
- [Object Attributes in OOUX](/glossary/object-attributes-ooux.html)
- [OOUX Prototyping and Testing](/glossary/ooux-prototyping-and-testing.html)

- [AI Prototyping](/glossary/ai-prototyping.html)

## Sources

- [OOUX Masterclass: Content Prototyping](https://ooux.com/selfpacedoouxmasterclass)
- [Contentful: Content Modeling Basics](https://www.contentful.com/help/content-models/content-modelling-basics/)

name: Conversational UX
contentMarkdown:
# Conversational UX

Conversational UX is the design of experiences in which people interact with a system through exchanges of language, using text, voice, or both. It covers how a conversation starts, progresses, handles misunderstandings, and helps a person complete a task.

## Conversational UX vs. conversation design

Conversation design focuses on the structure and content of the exchange: prompts, responses, turn-taking, and repair. Conversational UX also includes the surrounding experience, such as discovering capabilities, moving between chat and other controls, and reviewing outcomes.

A conversational interface does not require a generative model. It can use scripted flows, intent recognition, or a combination of techniques.

## Example: changing a travel date

A traveler asks, “Can I move this to Friday?” The system needs to establish which booking and which date the person means.

A useful response might show the identified booking, ask for the missing date, and present available options in a comparison view. Before applying a change, it shows the selected option and any relevant consequences.

If the traveler corrects the date, the system preserves the rest of the useful context. If no options are available, it provides a clear next step rather than restarting the conversation.

## What should designers specify?

| Moment | Design question |
|---|---|
| Entry | What can this system help the person do? |
| Clarification | Which missing detail is necessary now? |
| Response | Does the user need text, a choice, a table, or a form? |
| Correction | Can they change one detail without repeating everything? |
| Completion | Can they tell what happened and what remains? |

Write sample conversations for ordinary and difficult cases. Include ambiguous references, changed intent, interrupted tasks, and failed operations.

Conversation design concerns the exchange's underlying logic, including what happens when the system does not understand a request. Adding a text box or voice input does not define that logic.

## Conversational UX vs. agentic UX

A chat can answer questions without acting on another system. An agent may perform delegated work through chat, a task queue, or another interface.

When conversation leads to action, [agentic UX](/glossary/agentic-ux.html) adds questions about authorization, progress, review, interruption, and recovery.

Use direct controls when they make the task clearer. A calendar or comparison table can complement language; users should not have to describe every precise selection in prose.

## Related terms

- [Agentic UX](/glossary/agentic-ux.html)
- [Generative UI](/glossary/generative-ui.html)
- [AI-native Design](/glossary/ai-native-design.html)
- [Progressive Disclosure](/glossary/progressive-disclosure.html)

## Sources

- [What is conversation design?, Google (legacy guide)](https://developers.google.com/assistant/conversation-design/what-is-conversation-design)
- [Feedback and Control, Google PAIR](https://pair.withgoogle.com/chapter/feedback-controls/)

name: Design Critique
contentMarkdown:
# Design Critique

A design critique is a structured discussion intended to improve a design by examining how well it addresses a stated problem. Participants give feedback on the work and its reasoning, using the goals, evidence, and constraints relevant to the project.

## What should a critique accomplish?

Bring a specific question, such as whether an operations screen makes urgent exceptions visible. Share the audience, task, stage of work, known constraints, and decisions that remain open.

The group should understand what kind of feedback can change the design now. Reviewing a low-fidelity flow for color polish is unlikely to answer a question about its information structure.

## A lightweight critique process

| Step | What to do |
|---|---|
| Frame | Explain the task, evidence, constraints, and review question |
| Inspect | Let people understand the proposal and ask clarifying questions |
| Discuss | Connect observations to goals and likely user effects |
| Decide next steps | Separate fixes, alternatives, and questions needing research |

Name the decision owner. A critique can inform a decision without requiring a vote or unanimous agreement.

## Example: reviewing a dense operations table

Suppose the question is whether an operator can identify bookings awaiting a time-sensitive action.

“Make the status brighter” is a proposed solution. “The pending action is hidden among several unrelated status labels” identifies a problem to investigate.

The team can compare options: clearer grouping, a dedicated action field, filtering, or different emphasis. It checks these against realistic records and the operator's task.

Record assumptions that need user research. A room of colleagues agreeing that an option feels clearer does not establish that operators can use it successfully.

## Critique vs. usability testing vs. approval

A critique draws on the participants' expertise and available evidence. Usability testing observes representative people attempting tasks. Approval authorizes a decision or release.

These activities may inform one another, but they answer different questions. Make their purpose explicit so a critique is not treated as completed user validation.

## How do you make feedback actionable?

Describe the observation, its relevance, and the uncertainty. Ask why a decision was made before proposing a replacement. Focus on the work rather than the designer.

Keep a concise record of the decision, rationale, owner, and next action. When the group disagrees, identify what evidence could resolve the disagreement. This gives the next review a concrete starting point.

## Related terms

- [DesignOps](/glossary/designops.html)
- [Design QA](/glossary/design-qa.html)
- [Product Discovery](/glossary/product-discovery.html)
- [Design Strategy Alignment](/glossary/design-strategy-alignment.html)

## Sources

- [Design Critiques: Encourage a Positive Culture to Improve Products, NN/g](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/design-critiques/)
- [Analyse a research session, GOV.UK Service Manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/analyse-a-research-session)

name: ResearchOps
contentMarkdown:
# ResearchOps

ResearchOps, short for research operations, is the organization of the people, processes, tools, and resources that support research. It helps teams recruit participants, handle research material, coordinate studies, and make findings available for appropriate use.

## What does ResearchOps cover?

The exact responsibilities vary with the organization and its research program.

| Area | Typical operational work |
|---|---|
| Participants | Recruitment processes, scheduling, communication, and incentives |
| Consent and data | Approved handling, access, retention, and participant requests |
| Tools | Access, setup, evaluation, and support |
| Knowledge | Findable evidence, research records, and clear source context |
| Coordination | Shared calendars, support, and repeatable practices |
| Capability | Onboarding and support for people conducting research |

The ResearchOps Community describes a broad framework for supporting research across organizations. A small team can apply the relevant practices without creating a separate department.

## Example: repeated recruitment delays

Suppose several product teams repeatedly struggle to recruit the same type of participant. ResearchOps can help establish a shared recruitment process, clear eligibility criteria, scheduling support, and a record of prior participation.

Researchers still decide which participants fit each question and which method is appropriate. A reusable process should not quietly narrow every study to the easiest people to reach.

Review who is missing from the recruitment approach, including people with relevant access needs.

## ResearchOps vs. DesignOps vs. research

[DesignOps](/glossary/designops.html) supports the broader operation of design work. ResearchOps focuses on the conditions and infrastructure that make research possible and useful.

Conducting research includes defining questions, selecting methods, collecting evidence, and interpreting findings. Operational support enables that work; it does not replace the research judgment involved.

Responsibilities may overlap, and one person may perform several roles. Make ownership clear enough that a team knows where to get help.

## What changes when research tools use AI?

Review what material the tool receives, how it is handled, and how generated interpretations remain traceable to evidence. Maintain a distinction between participant statements and AI-produced summaries.

An automatically generated research repository still needs appropriate access, source references, and maintenance. Searchable findings can be misleading if they omit the study's date, sample, context, or limitations.

Start with a recurring bottleneck and evaluate whether the operational change improves research quality and access as well as reducing coordination effort.

## Related terms

- [DesignOps](/glossary/designops.html)
- [AI in UX Research](/glossary/ai-ux-research.html)
- [Synthetic User Testing](/glossary/synthetic-user-testing.html)
- [Product Discovery](/glossary/product-discovery.html)

## Sources

- [About ResearchOps, ResearchOps Community](https://researchops.community/about/)
- [ResearchOps 101, NN/g](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/research-ops-101/)
- [Getting informed consent for user research, GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research)

name: OOUX and ORCA
contentMarkdown:
# OOUX and ORCA

Explore the OOUX and ORCA glossary through the questions a product team needs to answer: what people work with, how those things connect, what users can do, and what information they need.

Start with [Object-Oriented UX](/glossary/object-oriented-ux.html) for the design approach and [ORCA Framework](/glossary/orca-framework.html) for the four iterative rounds. Then follow the [worked booking example](/glossary/ooux-worked-example.html) to see how the pieces fit together.

## Discover the product's structure

Use [Noun Foraging](/glossary/noun-foraging.html) to identify candidate objects from research. Investigate connections with a [Nested Object Matrix](/glossary/nested-object-matrix.html), actions with a [CTA Matrix](/glossary/cta-matrix.html), and information through [Object Mapping](/glossary/object-mapping.html).

[Object Attributes in OOUX](/glossary/object-attributes-ooux.html) explains core content, metadata, and the distinction between a field and a related object.

## Clarify requirements

An [Object Guide](/glossary/object-guide.html) records what each object means. [ORCA Relationship Requirements](/glossary/orca-relationship-requirements.html) examines how connections work, while [Cardinality](/glossary/cardinality-ux-architecture.html) clarifies permitted counts in both directions.

[Object-Oriented User Stories](/glossary/object-oriented-user-stories.html) develops the reason and conditions for an action. A [State Transition Matrix](/glossary/state-transition-matrix.html) can document the lifecycle behind it.

## Prioritize the release and the experience

These four activities address related decisions:

| Activity | Question |
|---|---|
| [Object Prioritization](/glossary/object-prioritization.html) | Which things need support, and how will users reach them? |
| [Relationship Prioritization](/glossary/relationship-prioritization.html) | Which connections and navigation paths matter for the task? |
| [CTA Prioritization](/glossary/cta-prioritization.html) | Which actions need support and prominence in this context? |
| [Attribute Prioritization](/glossary/attribute-prioritization.html) | Which information helps users identify, compare, and act? |

## Represent and test the model

[Object Representation](/glossary/object-representation-ooux.html) connects the model to cards, lists, and detailed views. A [Shapeshifter Matrix](/glossary/shapeshifter-matrix.html) helps document intentional variants.

Use the [Four UX Fails in OOUX](/glossary/ooux-ux-fails.html) as a diagnostic lens, [Content Prototyping](/glossary/content-prototyping.html) to populate the model, and [OOUX Prototyping and Testing](/glossary/ooux-prototyping-and-testing.html) to observe recognition, navigation, and action understanding.

## Work through more complex models

A [Junction Object](/glossary/junction-object.html) can represent a connection with its own information. [Tree Systems](/glossary/tree-systems-ooux.html) describes related forms that become more specific in context. [Object Inheritance in OOUX](/glossary/object-inheritance-ooux.html) examines general types and meaningful subtypes.

For surrounding practices, explore [Content Modeling](/glossary/content-modeling.html), [Domain Context Modeling](/glossary/domain-context-modeling.html), and [Structural Navigation Model](/glossary/structural-navigation-model.html).

To plan collaborative work, see [ORCA Sprint](/glossary/orca-sprint.html). Choose a bounded problem and use the relevant tools; revisit research whenever the model exposes an unanswered question.

## Sources

- [Sophia V. Prater: Introducing ORCA](https://medium.com/design-bootcamp/introducing-orca-the-third-diamond-in-your-ux-process-23a1babb0389)

name: OOUX Worked Example: A Booking Workflow
contentMarkdown:
# OOUX Worked Example: A Booking Workflow

This illustrative OOUX example follows a travel operations task from a research note to a testable interface. It uses ORCA's Objects, Relationships, Calls-to-Action, and Attributes to make the modeling and design decisions explicit.

The records and rules are fictional. They show one possible product scope, with assumptions that a real team would need to validate.

## Start with a task and evidence

Suppose a research walkthrough includes this statement:

> I find the trip, check which booking the traveler means, and ask the supplier to cancel it. I need to know whether the request is still waiting or the cancellation is complete.

The task is to identify the right booking, request an eligible cancellation, and understand the outcome. [Noun Foraging](/glossary/noun-foraging.html) suggests Trip, Booking, Traveler, and Supplier as candidates.

For this release, the team investigates Trip, Booking, and Traveler as separate record types. It retains supplier identification on a booking and defers a supplier-management workspace. That scope decision would change if operators need to manage supplier records.

## Discovery: build a small model

Trip T-104 has two travelers and two bookings. Booking B-52 is Confirmed; Booking B-53 is Awaiting confirmation.

| Object type | Representative information | Connection or action |
|---|---|---|
| Trip | Trip reference and travel dates | Contains bookings and associated travelers. |
| Booking | Booking reference, status, service date, supplier details | Belongs to one trip; an eligible agent can request cancellation. |
| Traveler | Identity and permitted contact information | Can be associated with multiple trips. |

This model allows a trip with no bookings and requires every booking to belong to one trip. A [Nested Object Matrix](/glossary/nested-object-matrix.html) and [CTA Matrix](/glossary/cta-matrix.html) can investigate relationships and actions systematically.

If eligibility depends on which traveler is covered by a service, the team must model that connection explicitly. Association with the same trip alone does not establish passenger coverage.

## Requirements: make the cancellation rule precise

For the example, the requesting agent must have access, be assigned to the trip, and act on an eligible confirmed booking.

The [object-oriented user story](/glossary/object-oriented-user-stories.html) adds the motivation: the traveler has changed plans, and the agent needs to start the supplier's cancellation process.

The expected sequence is:

1. Show the target booking and relevant conditions for review.
2. Submit an authorized cancellation request.
3. When the request is accepted for processing, show Cancellation pending and its reference.
4. Show Canceled only after the supplier confirms cancellation.

An already-pending request should remain inspectable. A submission timeout requires checking whether the request exists before retrying. If the supplier declines, show the result and current booking state.

Document these outcomes in the [State Transition Matrix](/glossary/state-transition-matrix.html). The application enforces the rules at execution.

## Prioritization: decide what the first release needs

| Decision area | Example choice |
|---|---|
| Objects | Support Trip, Booking, and Traveler; defer supplier profiles. |
| Relationships | Show a trip's bookings and a contextual route from a booking back to its trip. |
| Actions | Make eligible cancellation easy to find and provide access to pending requests. |
| Attributes | Emphasize booking reference, status, and service date in the work queue. |

The supplier confirmation number remains important even if a particular compact queue does not always display it. [Attribute Prioritization](/glossary/attribute-prioritization.html) separates required data from prominence in a view.

## Representation: preserve identity across views

A search result and a trip's booking list both identify B-52 with the same reference and status meaning. The detailed record adds relevant conditions, history, and permitted actions.

The cancellation review repeats the booking identity and proposed operation. Its completion message distinguishes a submitted request from a completed cancellation.

A [Shapeshifter Matrix](/glossary/shapeshifter-matrix.html) records why views differ. The goal is for users to recognize the booking while receiving the detail appropriate to the task.

## Test the model and interface

Populate a [content prototype](/glossary/content-prototyping.html) with the two bookings, an empty trip, and a record with missing conditional data.

Then ask representative users to find B-52 from a supplier message, identify its trip, respond to a cancellation need, and explain the state after submission. Include direct entry through search.

Observe mistaken identities, wrong routes, missed conditions, and misunderstandings about pending outcomes. These are proposed checks, not reported research findings.

Revise the relevant object definition, relationship, action rule, or representation. The [OOUX and ORCA reading path](/glossary/ooux/) links the methods behind each decision.

## Sources

- [Sophia V. Prater: Introducing ORCA](https://medium.com/design-bootcamp/introducing-orca-the-third-diamond-in-your-ux-process-23a1babb0389)
- [Nielsen Norman Group: Usability Testing 101](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/)
